references.text: The parable of the unmerciful servant also deals with debt and forgiveness. A servant owes the king an enormous sum, but has his debt forgiven – a parallel theme about unequal debts and grace as in Jesus' parable of the two debtors.

The immediate context for the parable of the two debtors: Jesus tells this parable to Simon the Pharisee to illustrate the connection between forgiveness and love, based on the woman who anointed Jesus' feet.
The parable of the unjust steward also contains motifs about debtors owing different amounts, and a master who has the power to forgive or demand repayment of the debt.
The Lord invites reconciliation and offers forgiveness for sin – a fundamental theme about God's willingness to forgive human debts, as illustrated by the parable of the two debtors.
In the Our Father we pray to have our debts (sins) forgiven, just as we also forgive our debtors. The same concept of sin as debt underlies Jesus' parable.

All have sinned and fall short of God's glory, but are justified freely by his grace. The parable of the two debtors illustrates this: both owe debts, and both depend on the lender forgiving the debt.
Jesus' prayer includes a request for forgiveness of sins, expressed as debt (ὀφείλοντι), using the same word field found in the parable of the two debtors.

The parable of the workers in the vineyard also shows a master who acts with unexpected generosity – those who worked little received the same as those who worked much – a parallel theme about grace that surpasses merit.
